summary:
NOVA/X is a browser-native, three-dimensional astronomical discovery application developed for the 2026 NASA International Space Apps Challenge, “Planet X and SPHEREx.” Its monochrome Mission Control interface transforms SPHEREx survey concepts into an interactive environment for researchers. SPHEREx observes the sky across 102 spectral channels, spanning 0.75–5.0 micrometers through six Linear Variable Filter detector arrays.

NOVA/X combines a Three.js 3D celestial and spectral-temporal viewport, a 102-band spectrophotometer, and a Temporal Blink and Difference Residual Engine (E₂ − E₁). Comparing observations from different epochs helps users investigate changes in an object's position and brightness. Difference mode suppresses stationary sources and reveals residual patterns associated with moving objects, including WISE 0855, Barnard’s Star, Epsilon Indi B, and a simulated Planet X candidate. It also explores variability in RW Aurigae and R Draconis.

Selecting an object displays its infrared spectrum and highlights molecular features associated with water (H₂O), methane (CH₄), carbon monoxide (CO), and carbon dioxide (CO₂). NOVA/X offers multi-mission catalog overlays and shareable links containing target coordinates and field-of-view settings. By combining 3D visualization, temporal comparison, and spectral exploration, NOVA/X makes astronomical data accessible and helps users investigate potential signals without presenting candidates as confirmed discoveries.
details:
NOVA/X is an interactive, three-dimensional astronomical discovery platform developed for the NASA International Space Apps Challenge to bridge the gap between vast, multi-epoch infrared sky surveys and human visual intuition. At its scientific core, the application explores some of modern astrophysics' most compelling questions: the search for elusive, cold objects in the outer Solar System, including the hypothesized Planet X (or Planet Nine) and ultra-cool brown dwarfs, as well as the tracking of transient and variable stellar phenomena over time. Rather than presenting researchers and citizen scientists with static tables of raw FITS pixel arrays, NOVA/X transforms multi-epoch near-infrared observations into a responsive, monochrome, three-dimensional environment where motion, brightness variability, and spectral characteristics can be explored together.

NOVA/X is designed as a browser-native Mission Control interface with an intentional high-contrast black-and-white aesthetic. Its layout separates analytical instruments from the central celestial viewport, ensuring that the visual workspace remains clear and accessible. The top navigation bar provides access to mission telemetry, display modes, shareable discovery URLs, the Judge Pitch, and the Science Brief. The left-hand console allows users to select six benchmark targets—WISE 0855, Barnard’s Star, Epsilon Indi B, RW Aurigae, R Draconis, and a simulated Planet X candidate—while configuring signal-to-noise enhancements and cross-mission catalog overlays. Beneath the central viewport sits the temporal blink and difference engine, while the right-hand panel displays a 102-band infrared spectrophotometer that updates when a celestial object is selected.

At the heart of NOVA/X is a custom WebGL simulation powered by Three.js, which provides two complementary ways to explore the cosmos. In the default 3D Celestial Sphere mode, the application constructs a celestial coordinate grid based on the International Celestial Reference System (ICRS J2000), populated by hundreds of background field stars and the primary benchmark targets. Users can navigate the scene through orbital camera controls, adjust the field of view, and select individual stars through interactive raycasting. Switching to the 3D Spectral-Temporal Cube transforms the sky into a volumetric data structure, where vertical pillars represent each object's integrated near-infrared flux and historical trajectory arcs illustrate archival WISE and NEOWISE astrometric observations spanning 2010 through 2024.

One of NOVA/X's central features is its interactive Temporal Blink and Difference Residual Engine, designed to make subtle changes in an object's position or brightness easier to recognize. By comparing observations from different epochs, users can investigate possible motion caused by proper motion or solar parallax. The interface allows users to scrub between Epoch 1 and Epoch 2, activate an automated blink comparator with adjustable timing, or enable mathematical difference mode using the equation D = E2 − E1. In difference mode, stationary background sources can be suppressed, while moving objects may appear as paired residual signals indicating their previous and current positions. Variable stars, on the other hand, may produce residual patterns due to changes in brightness even when their positions remain approximately constant. These visual differences help users investigate possible motion and photometric variability.

The platform also includes a 102-band near-infrared spectrophotometer modeled on SPHEREx's Linear Variable Filter detector architecture, covering wavelengths from 0.75 to 5.0 micrometers. When a user selects an object in the 3D viewport, the spectrometer displays its flux profile across the available channels, with interactive wavelength inspection in microjanskys. The interface highlights important molecular absorption regions that may help users investigate the characteristics of cold planetary and substellar atmospheres, including water-related features near 1.5, 2.0, and 3.0 micrometers, methane absorption near 3.3 micrometers, and carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide features between 4.2 and 4.7 micrometers.

To provide additional scientific context, NOVA/X incorporates multi-mission cross-matching and data-quality diagnostics. Users can activate a simulated six-band detector coaddition pass to demonstrate how combining observations may improve signal-to-noise, overlay Gaia Data Release 3 optical counterparts to investigate whether an infrared source has a visible optical counterpart, and inspect indicators for potential data-quality issues such as stray light, detector saturation, and South Atlantic Anomaly passage. The platform also includes URL state encoding, allowing users to share selected right ascension, declination, and field-of-view coordinates through a single link, alongside an integrated presentation guide explaining the physical characteristics of the six benchmark targets.

NOVA/X aims to make complex infrared astronomical observations more accessible, visual, and intuitive. By combining three-dimensional visualization, temporal comparison, spectral exploration, and multi-mission context, it creates an interactive environment for investigating possible astronomical signals. The platform is intended to serve as both a functional astronomical prototype and a scientific hackathon showcase. Its purpose is not to claim the discovery of Planet X or any other object, but to help users explore observational evidence, recognize interesting patterns, and better understand the scientific process behind astronomical discovery.
